 Podcast Episode: Christmas 2026 and New Year 2027 – when are the Bank Holidays and what about pay
 psimonparsons 
 Uncategorized 
 21st October 2026 
 2 Minutes 
 Pip: PAYadvice.UK — where the festive season preparation for payroll arrives in October, because payroll waits for no one.
 Mara: psimonparsons has been digging into the Christmas and New Year 2026 to 2027 bank holiday picture — when they fall, what employers owe, and how early payroll runs interact with Universal Credit.
 Pip: Let’s start with the bank holidays themselves and what paying early actually costs your workers.
 Christmas 2026 and New Year 2027: Bank Holidays and Early Pay
 Mara: The core question here is straightforward: when exactly are the bank holidays this Christmas, and what do employers actually have to do about pay — especially if they need to run payroll early?
 Pip: Boxing Day lands on a Saturday this year, so the substitute falls on Monday the 28th — and Scotland gets an extra wrinkle because the 2nd of January 2027 is also a Saturday, pushing that substitute to Monday the 4th.
 Mara: On the underlying entitlement, the post is direct: “Bank or public holidays do not have to be given as paid leave.”
 Pip: Which surprises people every year. The statutory minimum is 5.6 weeks of paid annual leave, and employers can count bank holidays inside that total rather than on top of it.
 Mara: It gets more complicated for irregular-hours workers. Those on rolled-up holiday pay have already received any holiday pay due in advance, so the actual leave dates may not attract additional payment. Workers accruing by hours worked need to draw down accrued leave to get paid for Christmas Day.
 Pip: So the day off might be free; the paid day off is a different negotiation entirely.
 Mara: Contracts matter here. Some employers do provide additional bank holiday entitlements above the statutory floor, and the post flags that policies need to be communicated clearly ahead of the season.
 Pip: Then there is the early payment question, which is where things get genuinely consequential for workers on Universal Credit.
 Mara: HMRC’s permanent easement — in place since 2019 — says that if you pay early over Christmas, you must still report your normal or contractual payment date on your Full Payment Submission. The post gives a concrete example: pay on the 20th of December, normal date is the 31st, report the 31st.
 Pip: Because if you report the early actual date instead, a UC claimant can see two payments land in one assessment period and nothing in the next — and the post describes that outcome plainly as devastation, not inconvenience.
 Mara: The post also points to ACAS guidance on employment rights for those who have to work over the Christmas and New Year period, covering what workers in that position are actually entitled to.
 Pip: Rights at work don’t take a holiday, even when everyone else does. Speaking of ongoing obligations — let’s think about what comes next in the payroll calendar.
 Mara: Bank holidays, rolled-up pay, RTI reporting, Universal Credit timing — a lot rides on decisions made quietly in December.
 Pip: Get the payment date wrong on a submission and someone’s benefits take the hit. Worth the ten-second check.
